rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.7 describe two lysimeter experiments (clayey Vertisol and dune sand) with lettuce under DI/SDI with and without oxygen-nanobubble TWW, own measurements of soil air O2, water content, CO2 flux, yield and physiology. Q2: Section 3.1 and Table 3 report that average soil air O2 at 10 cm under both DI and SDI with ONB-TWW significantly increased (p<0.03) in both soils (sand 18.9-19.2 to 19.2-19.3%; clay 16-18 to 19-20%); Section 4/Conclusions state ONB irrigation increased soil air O2 regardless of soil type and drip method. Q4: Section 3.1 measures DO added to the irrigation water (+14 mg/L, ~20 mg O2 per litre), estimates O2 stored in nanobubbles, and compares O2 delivered with daily O-CO2 emission (CO2 flux, Fig. SI-3, Table SI-1), i.e. an oxygen mass balance of the intermediate pathway; WFPS was also measured (Section 2.4, 3.2). Q8: Section 2.3 states the continuous O2 sensors in the clayey-soil lysimeters got flooded and could not provide accurate readings; Section 4 states it is hard to explain how the small O2 input elevated soil-air O2 and that the mechanism is not understood.
rows.notes: The passage lists several effects (mechanical strength, air permeability, air-filled porosity, soil aeration); the study only measures soil aeration as soil-air O2 concentration, and it is in lysimeters with oxygen-nanobubble treated wastewater, a form of aerated drip irrigation. Q3: two O2 measurement approaches existed in sand (periodic air extraction with O2 meter and continuous in-situ sensors), but results are not presented as cross-validation and sensors failed in clay, so treated as a single method. Q5: only two soils, one crop, one site. Q9: methods say data are means <U+00B1> SE, but Table 3 soil-air O2 values are reported without dispersion; Fig. 2 shows time series only, so no dispersion measure for the aeration result in the main text.

notes: Full text available; supplementary tables (SI-1 to SI-3) referenced but not included.
